questions.stem: On a Linux system, where are users' encrypted password hashes stored, and who can read that file?

choices.text: /etc/shadow; readable only by root (and processes with elevated rights)

questions.explanation: Encrypted passwords live in /etc/shadow, which standard users cannot read. /etc/passwd lists accounts but no longer holds the password hash on modern systems.
questions.trap: /etc/passwd is publicly readable but does NOT contain the actual hashes anymore; it just lists user metadata.

questions.stem: Which is the BEST-practice way to run a single administrative command on Linux without staying logged in as the superuser?

choices.text: su -, then run all commands as root for the rest of the session
Log in directly as root using SSH
sudo <command>, which elevates only that single command
Change ownership of the file with chown so root rights are not needed

questions.explanation: sudo elevates a single command. The transcript flags it as the preferred best practice over switching the whole session with su.
questions.trap: su switches your whole session to root, which keeps the elevated state alive longer than necessary.

questions.stem: A Linux admin runs 'chmod 764 file.sh'. What permissions does this grant?

choices.text: Owner: rwx, group: rw-, others: r--
Owner: rw-, group: r--, others: rwx
Owner: r--, group: rwx, others: rw-

questions.explanation: Octal: 4=r, 2=w, 1=x. 7=rwx, 6=rw, 4=r. So 764 = owner rwx, group rw, others r.
questions.trap: The order is always owner-group-others. Do not flip it.

questions.stem: Which Linux package manager is associated with each distribution family?

choices.text: apt on Red Hat; dnf on Debian/Ubuntu
apt on Debian/Ubuntu; dnf on Red Hat
Both apt and dnf are only on macOS
apt and dnf are only used on Windows Subsystem for Linux

questions.explanation: apt is Debian/Ubuntu's package manager. dnf is Red Hat's (RHEL/Fedora family).
questions.trap: The reversed claim (apt on Red Hat, dnf on Debian) is the trap; apt = Debian/Ubuntu, dnf = Red Hat.

questions.stem: A tech runs 'ping 8.8.8.8' on Linux. What is the default behavior?

choices.text: It sends exactly 4 packets then stops, like Windows
It fails because Linux ping does not exist
It requires sudo and refuses to run for normal users
It runs continuously until the user presses Ctrl+C

questions.explanation: Linux ping runs forever until stopped with Ctrl+C, unlike Windows' default 4 packets.
questions.trap: It is easy to assume ping behaves the same across OSes, but the default packet count differs.

questions.stem: Which command lists directory contents in a detailed view including hidden files and permissions?
questions.explanation: ls -la lists everything (including hidden files starting with a dot) in long format showing permissions, owner, size, and timestamp.
questions.trap: Plain ls shows only non-hidden file names without permissions or sizes.

questions.stem: Which Linux command provides a live, real-time dashboard of CPU and memory usage by running processes?
questions.explanation: top shows a real-time dashboard of CPU and memory usage by process.
questions.trap: ps -e gives a one-shot snapshot of every running process, not a live dashboard.

questions.stem: An admin wants to manually map a hostname to a specific IP, overriding DNS. Which file should they edit?
questions.explanation: /etc/hosts lets you statically map a domain name to an IP address and is consulted before DNS.
questions.trap: /etc/resolv.conf is the list of DNS servers; it does not contain individual hostname mappings.

questions.stem: On modern Linux, which component is responsible for managing background services (daemons)?
questions.explanation: After the kernel starts, systemd runs and manages all the background services (daemons) on modern Linux distributions.
questions.trap: GRUB is the bootloader that hands control to the kernel; it does not manage running services.

questions.stem: A Linux admin wants to see how much free disk space each mounted file system has, in a human-readable format. Which command?
questions.explanation: df -h shows free disk space per file system in human-readable units (KB/MB/GB).
questions.trap: du -h shows how much space a specific directory IS USING, not the free space on the file system.
